# Migration - Bottom Up

This simple examples uses three JAR files as shown in the following table.

| JAR File     | JAR Type | Loaded As | Dependencies | Main Method |
| ------------ | -------- | --------- | ------------ | :---------: |
| `app.jar`    | Regular  | Unnamed   | `domain.jar` |   **YES**   |
| `domain.jar` | Regular  | Automatic | `common.jar` |     No      |
| `common.jar` | Modular  | Named     | None         |     No      |

In the bottom-up migration, we start from the dependencies. We will start from
the `common.jar` JAR file as this has no other dependencies.

The `domain.jar` can be loaded from the class path, as code within the *unnamed*
module can access code within a *named* module. This example chose to load the
`domain.jar` using the `--module-path`, thus as an *automatic* module, so that
it illustrates a shortcoming of the *automatic* modules. The *automatic*
modules do not contain the `module-info.java` file thus the Java Module System
cannot determine what other modules are required. This information needs to be
provided at runtime using the `--add-modules` command line option.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

## Run the example

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the JAR files were created and copied to the
   `./target/libs` and `./target/mods` directories.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name --prune -P '*.jar' './target'
   ```

   The application JAR files

   ```
   ./target
   ├── libs
   │   └── app.jar
   └── mods
       ├── common.jar
       └── domain.jar

   3 directories, 3 files
   ```

2. List all modules

   ```shell
   java --module-path './target/mods' --list-modules
   ```

3. Describe the JAR files

   ```shell
   jar --describe-module --file './target/mods/common.jar'
   ```

   The common module description

   ```
   demo.common@1.0.0 jar:file:///./target/mods/common.jar!/module-info.class
   exports demo.common
   requires java.base mandated
   ```

   ```shell
   jar --describe-module --file './target/mods/domain.jar'
   ```

   The domain module description

   ```
   No module descriptor found. Derived automatic module.

   demo.domain automatic
   requires java.base mandated
   contains demo.domain
   ```

   ```shell
   jar --describe-module --file './target/libs/app.jar'
   ```

   The application module description

   ```
   No module descriptor found. Derived automatic module.

   app automatic
   requires java.base mandated
   contains demo.app
   main-class demo.app.Main
   ```

4. Run the application

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     --module-path './target/mods' \
     demo.app.Main
   ```

   The application fails to launch because the application module does not
   require the domain module, so it is not loaded.

   ```
   Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: demo/domain/Quote
       at demo.app.Main.main(Main.java:7)
   Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: demo.domain.Quote
       at java.base/jdk.internal.loader.BuiltinClassLoader.loadClass(BuiltinClassLoader.java:580)
       at java.base/java.lang.ClassLoader.loadClass(ClassLoader.java:490)
       ... 1 more
   ```

   Add the `demo.domain` module using the `--add-modules` command line option.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     --module-path './target/mods' \
     --add-modules demo.domain \
     demo.app.Main
   ```

   This too fails as the automatic modules do not have the `module-info.java`
   file. Thus, the Java Module System cannot determine what modules these depend
   on. Thus, their dependencies needs to be added too to the `--add-modules`
   command line option.

   ```
   Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: demo/common/StringUtils
       at demo.domain/demo.domain.Quote.<init>(Quote.java:8)
       at demo.app.Main.main(Main.java:7)
   Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: demo.common.StringUtils
       at java.base/jdk.internal.loader.BuiltinClassLoader.loadClass(BuiltinClassLoader.java:580)
       at java.base/java.lang.ClassLoader.loadClass(ClassLoader.java:490)
       ... 2 more
   ```

   Add both the *automatic* module `demo.domain` and the *named* module
   `demo.common` using the `--add-modules` command line option.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     --module-path './target/mods' \
     --add-modules demo.domain,demo.common \
     demo.app.Main
   ```

   This time the application works and prints the following.

   ```
   Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow. The important thing is not to stop questioning. by Albert Einstein
   ```

   Given that we need to include all modules found on the module path, then we
   can simply use the `ALL-MODULE-PATH` option.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     --module-path './target/mods' \
     --add-modules ALL-MODULE-PATH \
     demo.app.Main
   ```

   The application works the same and prints the following.

   ```
   Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow. The important thing is not to stop questioning. by Albert Einstein
   ```

5. (*Optional*) Load the `domain.jar` from the class path as part of the
   *unnamed* module.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*:./target/mods/domain.jar' \
     --module-path './target/mods/common.jar' \
     --add-modules demo.common \
     demo.app.Main
   ```

   Note that this time only the `demo.common` has to be added as both `app.jar`
   and `domain.jar` are part of the *unnamed* module.

   This will produce the same result as before.

   ```
   Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow. The important thing is not to stop questioning. by Albert Einstein
   ```
